lessons.title: Survival kit: phrases for daily life in Korea

vocab.en: I'm not sure / I don't know

grammar.explanation:
주세요 is the polite way to say "please give me" or "please do it for me". It comes from 주다 (to give). It is the most useful request pattern for daily life in Korea: ordering food, shopping, taking taxis and asking for help.

To ask for a thing, put the noun first and then 주세요: 커피 주세요 (coffee, please). To say how many, put the number after the noun: 봉투 하나 주세요 (one bag, please). Adding 좀 (a little) before 주세요 makes it softer: 물 좀 주세요. The object marker 를/을 is usually dropped in these short requests.

To ask someone to do something, use the verb's ~아/어 form (taught properly in Lesson 6) and then 주세요: 말하다 → 말해 → 말해 주세요 (please say it); 가다 → 가 → 가 주세요 (please go); 내리다 → 내려 → 내려 주세요 (please let me off). For now you can learn these as fixed phrases.

examples.en: Please let me off over there.

grammar.explanation:
Use this to ask where something is. Say the place, add the subject marker 이/가, then 어디예요? 어디 means "where" and 예요 is the polite "is" (Lesson 1).

Pick the marker by the last sound of the place word. If it ends in a consonant, use 이: 화장실 → 화장실이 어디예요? If it ends in a vowel, use 가: 출구 (exit) → 출구가 어디예요?

In everyday speech the marker is often dropped: 화장실 어디예요? Both are fine. If you are lost, 여기가 어디예요? asks "where am I?" (literally "where is here?").

examples.note: 출구 ends in a vowel, so it takes 가.
The marker is dropped, as is common in speech.

examples.en: Where am I? (Where is this place?)

grammar.explanation:
Korean changes the end of a sentence to show how polite you are being. As a visitor you need two polite styles.

The ~요 style is everyday polite speech. Use it with shop staff, strangers, taxi drivers and colleagues: 얼마예요?, 괜찮아요, 맛있어요. If you only learn to speak one style, make it this one.

The ~습니다/ㅂ니다 style is formal. You hear it in announcements, from staff greeting customers, and in set phrases like 감사합니다, 죄송합니다 and 잘 먹겠습니다. Questions in this style end in ~습니까/ㅂ니까.

You don't need to produce the formal style yet, but learn to recognise it. The same idea can come in both styles: 감사합니다 and 감사해요 both mean "thank you".

examples.note: A subway announcement, in the formal style.
